title: AI Engineering as a Discipline
summary: Analyze the feedback loops of the ML system lifecycle and explain how they manage degradation.

blocks.md:
By the end of this lesson you should be able to:

- Analyze the feedback loops of the ML system lifecycle and explain how they manage degradation
- Explain why benchmark accuracy does not carry over to deployment populations that differ from evaluation data
- Classify the sequential stages of the ML system lifecycle
- Explain the disciplinary emergence and core mandate of AI engineering
- Quantify the multi-order-of-magnitude memory and compute span across cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML deployment paradigms

blocks.source: Vol I, Introduction, § AI Engineering as a Discipline
blocks.md: A cloud service may optimize throughput across racks of accelerators, while an edge device must remain within a strict battery and thermal envelope, so the same model can be efficient in one setting and unusable in another. An engineer who must hold predictive quality and resource cost to one specification across such different operating budgets needs to combine three quantitative tools.

blocks.title: What the section covers
blocks.md:
In the book this section runs through:

- Engineering across the ML lifecycle
- Deployment context shapes the lifecycle

Pay attention to: AI engineering definition (stochastic behavior under deterministic reliability); six-stage ML lifecycle and two core feedback loops; deployment paradigms and production case studies (Waymo, FarmBeats, AlphaFold).

blocks.prompt: Think first: The chapter compares AI engineering with the earlier emergence of computer engineering. What do the two disciplines share, and what does AI engineering add?
blocks.md: Both combine methods from established disciplines around a common set of requirements: computer engineering joined digital circuits, processor design, and software, so that moving a function between hardware and software could be judged by speed, power, and flexibility. AI engineering extends that shared design problem to learned behavior and the data that shapes it. Its requirements can be fixed, such as a recall target over a stated population, while the evidence that a system meets them stays statistical and must be reassessed as operating conditions change.

questions.q: The ML project responsibilities run from Problem Definition through Data Collection & Preparation, Model Development & Training, Evaluation & Validation, Deployment & Integration, and Monitoring & Maintenance. Which feedback pattern correctly interprets the finer-grained pipeline shown in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. Failed evaluation and production warnings initiate investigation against the requirements established during Problem Definition. A data coverage problem can return work to collection or preparation; a pipeline defect may need a software repair, and a model limitation may need a model update. Drift alone does not establish quality loss or select retraining. Any selected update passes through evaluation before redeployment. The figure separates collection from preparation to show pipeline detail, while the six project responsibilities include the upstream task definition.
questions.hint: Think about: analyze the feedback loops of the ML system lifecycle and explain how they manage degradation.
options: Deployment returns to Training on compiler warnings, and Collection returns to Preparation on memory leaks.
Monitoring returns to Deployment on network timeouts, and Preparation returns to Collection on syntax errors.
Evaluation can return work to preparation when investigation identifies a data problem, and monitoring can motivate new collection when outcome evidence and diagnosis identify a coverage gap.
Model Training returns to Hardware Design on arithmetic overflow, and Deployment returns to Operating System Kernel on driver faults.

questions.q: The chapter uses autonomous driving to show a challenge that production ML systems share. What does the Waymo Open Dataset's report of domain gaps among San Francisco, Phoenix, and Mountain View imply for engineering such a system?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The gaps show that evaluation inputs and deployment inputs can differ, and a model's measured accuracy holds only for the population it was evaluated on. Where perception runs does not change what inputs the model sees. Retraining from scratch per city is one possible remedy, not what the evidence implies, and the gaps reflect real differences in driving environments rather than labeling mistakes.
questions.hint: Think about: explain why benchmark accuracy does not carry over to deployment populations that differ from evaluation data.
options: A model that scores well on inputs from one setting can lose accuracy where deployment inputs differ, so every remote update must be revalidated against the population it will meet.
Domain gaps disappear once perception runs on the vehicle rather than in the cloud, because local execution removes network effects.
Domain gaps show that a perception model must be retrained from scratch for each city before any deployment is possible.
Domain gaps are labeling errors that a larger annotation budget eliminates, after which one evaluation covers every city.

questions.q: Place the six ML project responsibilities in their initial progression from defining the task to maintaining the deployed system:
questions.explanation:
The correct order is (4) -> (5) -> (2) -> (1) -> (6) -> (3).
- (4) Problem Definition: Specify the task, operating population, constraints, and acceptance requirements.
- (5) Data Collection & Preparation: Gather representative evidence and construct the inputs used for learning.
- (2) Model Development & Training: Choose and train a model within the resource budget.
- (1) Evaluation & Validation: Assess task quality and system requirements under a stated protocol.
- (6) Deployment & Integration: Integrate the validated artifact into its operating environment.
- (3) Monitoring & Maintenance: Gather production evidence and diagnose whether earlier work needs revision.
This is an initial progression, not a rule that every alert repeats every stage.
questions.hint: Think about: classify the sequential stages of the ML system lifecycle.

questions.q: Across the four deployment paradigms in the chapter (Cloud, Edge, Mobile, TinyML), approximately what orders-of-magnitude span exists between the highest tier (Cloud) and the lowest tier (TinyML) in memory capacity and compute throughput?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. The deployment spectrum spans approximately five orders of magnitude (\$10^5\times$) in memory capacity (from $\approx 10^{11}\text{ bytes}$ in cloud accelerator nodes down to $\approx 10^6\text{ bytes}$ in TinyML microcontrollers) and six orders of magnitude (\$10^6\times$) in compute throughput (from $\approx 10^{15}\text{ ops/s}$ in cloud down to $\approx 10^9\text{ ops/s}$ in TinyML). This divergence of five to six orders of magnitude prevents arbitrary model transfer across tiers. Compression or redesign may be needed, and the resulting model must satisfy the target memory, timing, energy, and quality requirements. Spans of \$10^2$ or \$10^3$ drastically underestimate the divergence between cloud data centers and microcontrollers, while spans of \$10^{12}$ to \$10^{15}$ exceed physical realities.
questions.hint: Think about: quantify the multi-order-of-magnitude memory and compute span across cloud, edge, mobile, and TinyML deployment paradigms.
options: \$10^2$ (100$\times$) span in memory capacity and \$10^3$ (1,000$\times$) span in compute throughput
\$10^3$ (1,000$\times$) span in memory capacity and \$10^4$ (10,000$\times$) span in compute throughput
\$10^{12}$ (one trillion$\times$) span in memory capacity and \$10^{15}$ span in compute throughput
\$10^5$ (100,000$\times$) span in memory capacity and \$10^6$ (one million$\times$) span in compute throughput

questions.q: A team designing a battery-powered smart doorbell vision system chooses a TinyML microcontroller node over a cloud-offloaded architecture. What primary constraint tradeoff drove this architectural decision?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is A. The stated design prioritizes battery operation, local privacy, and independence from intermittent connectivity, accepting a small memory envelope. Local execution avoids sending the visual inputs needed for remote inference, but the chosen model must still fit and meet its timing and energy budgets. Cloud execution is computationally feasible; its complete cost includes radio transfers, network delay, and remote inference, with transfer energy depending on frame volume and duty cycle. Microcontrollers still require dataset curation and evaluation.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate the constraint trade-offs governing TinyML microcontroller deployments versus cloud architectures.
options: The doorbell must operate under a strict milliwatt power envelope on battery while preserving user visual privacy and avoiding reliance on intermittent wireless connectivity, accepting severe kilobyte-scale memory limits.
TinyML microcontrollers provide higher FP16 peak FLOP/s throughput than multi-GPU cloud nodes.
Cloud-based serving architectures cannot support visual wake-word classification algorithms.
Microcontrollers eliminate the need for dataset annotation and model evaluation.

points: You can now analyze the feedback loops of the ML system lifecycle and explain how they manage degradation.
You can now explain why benchmark accuracy does not carry over to deployment populations that differ from evaluation data.
You can now classify the sequential stages of the ML system lifecycle.
You can now explain the disciplinary emergence and core mandate of AI engineering.
